newsitem.title: USA: US rate jitters seen eroding Argentina's appeal.
newsitem.headline: US rate jitters seen eroding Argentina's appeal.

text.p: The prospect of further American interest rises this year is eroding Argentina's attractiveness to certain U.S. investors, New York-based Latin American market experts said.
They said Argentina is perceived as being particularly vulnerable to any further Fed increases because its currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar.
On April 8, Salomon Brothers cited the heightened probability of two further Fed hikes by midyear as a factor in its recommendation to underweight Argentina in its Latin American model portfolio.

"Although Argentina has held up well so far, we think that the market will have trouble staging much of an advance in this (U.S. interest rate) environment," Salomon Latin American equity analysts John Mullin wrote.

At Morgan Stanley, Latin America economist Ernest Brown estimated a U.S. federal funds rate rise to 6.5 percent by the end of the year from the current 5.5 percent threatened to lop one percentage point in Argentine gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1997.
"Like the law of gravity, rising interest rates in the dollar market will attract the liquidity flow from the peso market," he said.
While Salomon's Mullin forecast Argentine GDP growth at 5.2 percent this year, he said financial markets are turning lukewarm for the simple reason that the growth has already been priced in.
"The investors always try to stay ahead of the curve," he explained.
Under this scenario, the Argentine annual growth rate is likely to slow to 3.5 percent in the second half of 1997 from 6.1 percent in the first quarter and 5.3 percent in the second quarter.
"Things will look better for a while before they turn worse," Brown said.
On the credit front, Brown said it was naive to assume that domestic sources would compensate for tighter foreign credit despite ample liquidity in Argentine financial institutions.

Omar Borla, chief Latin America economist at Robert Flemings, had a positive outlook on Argentina's GDP, citing momentum from the GDP's 4.4 percent growth in 1996 after a 4.6 percent contraction in 1995.

With benefits from last year's recovery spreading through the economy, the job market in the service and manufacturing sectors have shown signs of improvement and to push the economy to the next phase of consumption-based growth, he said.
"The growth is moving above trendline," he said. "There is no deceleration."
Even so, Borla said he perceived dimming market interest in Argentina.
A solid GDP increase this year was not sufficient to excite investors because they had already taken the growth into account.

Analysts generally agreed that the current cycle of recovery in Argentina is more solid than the 1991-1994 recovery, which came to an abrupt end when the U.S. Federal Reserve started a series of rate increases while the Tequila effect of Mexico's December 1994 devaluation hit Latin America's markets.
Fixed-income sources agreed that positive fundamental news, that culminated in the upgrade of sovereign credit by Standard & Poor's Corp on April 2, have been discounted.

The Brady and Eurobond markets basically shrugged off the upgrade. In April, the Latin component of J.P. Morgan's broad emerging market bond index (EMBI+) rose 0.44 percent, while the Argentina subindex rose only 0.31 percent.
By contrast in 1996 the Argentine EMBI+ subindex rose 25 percent.

With fewer positive fundamentals anticipated, investors will tend to look more crtically at the vulnerability of the Argentine economy, such as the high debt burden and overvalued currency, they said.
In addition, Argentina's increasing dependence on Brazilian demand for its export growth in the past year provokes increasing concern if Brazil reins in its trade deficits, the sources said.
"Investors never overlooked those factors ... which become more important when the mood changes." an emerging market bond trader said.
